title: Lech Lecha: the road ran everywhere
hookLine: a man leaves home, and his family's road runs to Kochi, Mumbai and the mountains of Ethiopia

cards: Three scenes. In Kochi, on the southwest coast of India, a synagogue more than four hundred years old has a floor of hand-painted blue and white tiles from China.
Up the coast near Mumbai, a community of oil pressers was known for generations by a nickname: the Saturday oil-men, because they would not work on Saturday.
And in the mountains of Ethiopia, once a year, people climb to a high place in white clothes to pray and renew a promise. Every one of these is a Jewish scene.
Today's portion opens with the man whose leaving started it all.

teach.b: You met the call itself on day thirty-seven: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house." And then, simply: "So Abram went."
The family story of the Jewish people begins with someone leaving home, and the road didn't stop with him.
Over the centuries Jewish families settled almost everywhere, and each community kept the same Torah while cooking, singing and dressing like its neighbors.
You may know the Ashkenazi branch best: central and eastern Europe, Yiddish, the words you met on day three.
Sephardi Jews trace their families to Spain and Portugal, and after 1492 carried their Judeo-Spanish language across the Mediterranean.
Mizrahi Jews lived for many centuries in Iraq, Iran, Yemen, Syria and North Africa; the Jews of Iraq trace their community back to the exile in Babylon. In India there are several communities.
The Jews of Cochin, with that tiled synagogue.
The Bene Israel near Mumbai, whose tradition says their ancestors were shipwrecked on the coast long ago, and who kept Shabbat when they had almost nothing else.
And Baghdadi Jews, traders who came later to Mumbai and Kolkata.
In Ethiopia, the Beta Israel kept the Torah in the old Ge'ez language, led by their own priests, and fifty days after Yom Kippur they climb a mountain for the festival of Sigd.
Today many of these families live in Israel, North America and around the world. So if Jewish brings to mind bagels and Yiddish, that's real, and it's one branch of a very big tree.

how: Jewish communities around the world, Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi, Indian, Ethiopian and many more, read the same weekly Torah portion, each with its own melodies, foods, customs and languages.

o: come back, a call to return to your homeland
go forth, the call that sends Abram from home
a wanderer, someone who has no home at all

games.q: the Bene Israel oil pressers could earn more by working seven days. what did they do?
o: worked every day like everyone else.
rested on Saturday, and got a nickname for it.
moved their rest day to Sunday.
games.why: they kept Shabbat, and their neighbors called them the Saturday oil-men.

practice: Picture a map of the world, starting where Abram started, between two rivers.
Let little lights come on: Kochi, Mumbai, Baghdad, Sana'a, Fez, Seville, Vilna, a mountain in Ethiopia, a street near you, each a kitchen, a synagogue, a family keeping Shabbat its own way.
Stay with whichever one surprises you; if you pray, pray for every one of those tables.

wordCard.voice: Lech Lecha. Go forth: the call to Abram, and the start of a road that led Jewish families to nearly every corner of the world.

orig.note: Hebrew: go forth, literally go, for yourself; the call to Abram and the name of the portion.

carryVoice: Your line: the road ran everywhere. One man left home, and his family's story now speaks many languages. Day one hundred seventy-one.
